Peak Poker Performance

    It is not surprising that he would feel that falling into a deep, dark de-
pression was a possibility as a result of his long-term downswing. We now
know that a key trigger of depression is the brain’s runaway stress re-
sponse. When you experience a stressor, like a downswing, your brain
springs into action with an array of adaptations that are designed to pre-
pare you to tackle the threat. It’s important to note that the brain’s stress
response is ancient from an evolutionary perspective. It was designed to
deal with the kinds of short, intense stressors that our ancestors would
have had to deal with. It’s not well suited to the types of stressors that
we face today – like downswings, computer problems, or traffic jams.
    Think about it like this. In the old days, the stress response (or fight or
flight response, as it is better known) was quite useful. If you were out on
the plains hunting and gathering, most of the stressors you faced would
be of the predator type or perhaps a weather emergency. In those types
of situations, the appropriate response to stress would be an immediate
physical reaction. Running away or mounting a physical defense of some
sort was undoubtedly the best solution. Our brain is still calibrated in this
fashion, so when we experience chronic stressors, a variety of physical
reactions occur to prepare the body for an intense burst of action.
    The first thing that happens when we get stressed out is that the brain
calls for the release of a couple of potent hormones: adrenaline and corti-
sol. These then set into motion a whole other set of physical reactions. For
example, the liver dumps its stores of sugar into your bloodstream in order
to provide fuel for your muscles. Similarly your lungs increase their intake
of oxygen, and your heart beats faster and stronger. Even more troubling is
the fact that the stress response affects sleep. If you are under stress, your
sleep will be much more shallow and restless than when you are relaxed.
There is a steady disappearance of deep slow-wave sleep, which is the
type of sleep that is very restful. If you have more than a few nights of
slow-wave sleep deprivation, you will see the effects in the form of con-
centration lapses, negative mood, and even physical illness.
    As you might guess, the off switch for the stress response is the com-
pletion of an intense physical action. An intense burst of physical activity

                       Neuropsychology and Peak Poker Performance

provides direct feedback to the brain telling it that it can shut off the re-
sponse. Downswings, however, are not acute stressors. They are chronic
and last for a long time. When you are running bad, you are confronted
with days, weeks, or even months of pressure and losses. This keeps the
brain’s stress response clicked on in high gear.
   When we experience a stress response over a long period of time, it
starts to affect our brain in many negative ways. In particular, the frontal
cortex (the part of your brain right behind your eyeballs and forehead) is
dramatically affected. The frontal cortex is divided down the middle into a
right and left hemisphere, which play distinct and complementary roles in
shaping our mood. When the left hemisphere is more active than the
right, we become more goal oriented and our moods tend to be positive.
When the left hemisphere becomes less active, moods turn negative, goal
pursuit stops, and we become focused on avoiding harm. (This is how it
works if you are right handed; if you are left handed then your hemi-
spheres can be wired the other way around.)
   I’m sure you have guessed already how the brain operates when you
are under chronic stress: the left hemisphere of your frontal cortex shows
a dramatic decrease in activity and depression is a real possibility. At the
very least, you will probably feel irritated, unhappy, and unmotivated. As
an aside, prolonged exposure to cortisol also affects your memory. In
fact, this extended exposure can lead to the shrinkage of those parts of
your brain, which leads to problems with not only memory but also con-
centration, attention, and even abstract reasoning.
   As you can see, running bad for an extended period of time can have
profoundly negative effects on your brain. Once we experience the stress
of a few losing sessions, our brain chemistry and structure changes in
ways that make it likely we will start to spiral downward, and that can be
difficult to turn around. There are some things you can do to reverse the
trend though, and I’ll cover that material in the next couple of chapters.
For now, I want to talk a bit about the general negativity bias of the brain,
and the role it plays in loss aversion.

Peak Poker Performance

Negativity Bias
I would be remiss if I didn’t point out that the brain is naturally wired to
pay more attention to negative information than positive. This is the so
called negativity bias. The amygdala is wired to attend to emotional in-
formation, and results in an automatic emotional response that happens
very quickly and is mostly unconscious. While the amygdala pays atten-
tion to negative material in a general way, the dorsal anterior cingulate
(also a part of your limbic system) pays particular attention to mistakes
you make and to times when it thinks something might go wrong. It helps
the amygdala find reasons to freak out. Remember this the next time you
are running bad. Keep in mind that if you lean towards depression or anxi-
ety, you will experience more emotionality than people who do not have
such leanings. People with depression tend to fixate longer on emotional
information, which cuts down on their ability to be calm and rational.
    Even if you are not depressed, keep in mind that all brains react more
strongly to negative events than to positive ones. There is a concept called
loss aversion, which explains that losing something hurts more than gaining
something. I’m sure you have noticed that losing a $100 pot feels worse
than winning a $100 pot feels good. This is the negativity bias in action.
    Sabrina Tom (2007) conducted an experiment to see how the brain
evaluates risk. Brain scans of people who had a 50/50 chance of winning
a bet for a small amount of cash showed that a broad range of brain areas
lit up as the potential gains increased, but the same areas dimmed as po-
tential losses increased. Individuals with more pronounced levels of this
neural “loss aversion” had what could be considered more loss-averse
sensitive brains. If you really feel the pain of losing, you may have a more
loss-averse sensitive brain, as well!
    Some players’ brains are wired to react more deeply than those of oth-
ers to losses and disappointments. If depression runs in your family you
are more likely to have a brain that reacts strongly to losing money. One
interesting study found that people who are at risk of depression and who
lost money unexpectedly experienced greater activity in the prefrontal
cortex associated with lower motivation. When this group won money

                       Neuropsychology and Peak Poker Performance

unexpectedly it did not encode as a memory in their hippocampus. This is
a double edged sword because those people felt the sting of the loss and
were less likely to remember the times they won. People who suffer from
a very strong negativity bias show improvement when they experience
increases in the neurotransmitter serotonin and norepinephrine (which I
wrote about earlier in this chapter). So there is hope.

Summary
While the brain has many structures, only a few are of particular interest
to us. The most relevant structures to poker are the amygdala, the hippo-
campus, and the hypothalamus. Your hypothalamus runs many automatic
functions, and releases hormones that instigate the fight, flight, or freeze
mechanism when you are under stress. The hippocampus is involved in
memory, and the amygdala is your emotional center. Some neuropsy-
chologists call the limbic system the panic button, because it responds so
strongly to any perceived threat whether real or imagined. These areas all
talk to one another and generate your bodily states (emotions and feel-
ings) as well as physiological responses.
   There is a lot to the human brain and what I’ve written here only
scratches the surface! Just remember, you have an incredible number of
connections and a large number of neural circuits that are always working
for or against you. We are starting to learn more about how the brain
works, and it’s very encouraging. We now know that we can wire the
brain to do the things that we want it to do. Even if you have never been
a math person, for example, you can train your brain to learn poker math.
It may not be easy, but it is doable. The field of neuroscience is very dy-
namic, and I have no doubt that we will be learning even more about the
brain in the coming years.

Chapter Highlights

Peak Poker Performance

   ♠ The prefrontal cortex is responsible for willpower, planning, goal
       setting, decision making, evaluating right from wrong, and making
       predictions based off previous experiences.
   ♠ The prefrontal cortex is also where you reason about your
       emotions, regulate their intensity, control them, and adjust to
       other people’s emotions.
   ♠ The limbic system manages your circadian rhythm (sleep–wake
       cycle), emotions, hunger, and sex hormones.
   ♠ By releasing various hormones, the hypothalamus moderates your
       sleep, body temperature, and food and liquid intake.
   ♠ The hippocampus is responsible for consolidating learning and
       converting information from your working memory into long-term
       memory.
   ♠ The amygdala is so closely linked to the hippocampus that strong
       emotional events are readily encoded into memory.
   ♠ Neurons are the brain cells that allow us to think, feel, move,
       breathe, and do everything else that makes us human.
   ♠ Your brain changes as you learn new skills or habits using a process
       known as neuroplasticity.
   ♠ Neurogenesis and neuroplasticity can be fostered through
       essential habits.
   ♠ The amygdala and prefrontal cortex play key roles in how and why
       we tilt.

                       Neuropsychology and Peak Poker Performance

in topics they are actually clueless about. It has been documented that
“experts” in a given field feel as if their expertise transfers over to other
fields, which couldn’t be further from the truth. For example, the fact that
I am good at poker should not make me think that I am good at chess.
    I am sure you have sat at the poker table and heard players discuss
various topics as if they were experts. It is common to hear marginal
players discuss strategy as if they know exactly what they are talking
about. For what it’s worth, if someone is discussing strategy at the table,
they usually aren’t too good at poker.
    One time I was playing a $1,000 event in Las Vegas, and I overheard
an incredibly comical discussion. Phil Hellmuth was at the final table of a
WSOP event that started the next day at 4pm. Someone at my table
asked when his final table was going to take place. Another player, who
clearly thought he was amazing at everything, immediately chimed in and
said Phil was actually at a WPT final table that was taking place the next
day at 6pm (I don’t think a WPT final table has ever started at 6pm). He
was extremely confident. The person who asked the question (and a few
other people at the table) assumed he must know what he was talking
about, likely because he was so sure in his response.
    To succeed at poker it is vitally important that you are self-aware (the
guy who answered the question was clearly a losing player). If you think
you know something but in reality you are clueless, you will make huge
errors and make yourself look like a fool to the actual experts.
    For those who are new to the concept of self-awareness, or have
come to the conclusion that they lack self-awareness, it may be difficult
to figure out what you know and what you don’t. I suggest you start by
assuming you know nothing. Find experts and discuss any topic relevant
to what you are trying to become an expert at. For example, if you think
raising the flop with top pair, bad kicker is a good play but every expert
you talk with says it is a horrible play, assuming you cannot back up your
claim with math, you are probably incorrect. You should also study every-
thing produced by experts that you possibly can. For example, if you want
to learn about psychology, study psychology. Do not think that simply be-
